title: Birthday Jewelry She'll Actually Wear Every Day
excerpt: Forget the drawer jewelry. Here's how to pick a gift she'll reach for again and again.

content.text: The hardest part of giving jewelry as a gift isn't finding something beautiful — it's finding something she'll actually wear. A lot of jewelry sits in boxes because it feels too fancy, too delicate, or too specific to one outfit. If you want her to think of you every time she puts something on, you need a piece that fits into her real life, not just special occasions.

The best birthday gifts are the ones that become part of someone's everyday routine. That means waterproof, tarnish-resistant, and designed for movement. It means something that works with jeans as easily as it works with a dress. It means jewelry that doesn't require babying.
Skip the Delicate — Go for Durable

If she showers with her jewelry, jumps in the pool, or just lives in her accessories, delicate pieces aren't going to cut it. You want high-quality stainless steel that won't tarnish, won't turn her skin green, and won't snap after a few months. The right material matters more than you think — it's the difference between a gift that gets worn and a gift that gets boxed up.

Look for pieces that are built for everyday life. Body chains and anklets that stay put through movement. Bracelets that won't lose their shine after a beach day. Necklaces that work under t-shirts and sweaters, not just against bare skin. If it can survive her actual life, it's a keeper.
Personalized Pieces Hit Different

Generic jewelry is fine. Personalized jewelry is what she'll wear on repeat. That could mean her birthstone, her zodiac sign, her birth flower, or just her initial. The difference is personal — it's custom to her, not to anyone else. It shows you paid attention to who she is, not just what looks good.

Birthstone bracelets are a classic for a reason. Zodiac charm bracelets work for people who love astrology. Birth flower bracelets are perfect if she's into something a little different. Even something as simple as an initial bracelet makes it feel like it was made for her. When you browse the shop, you'll see these options available for most pieces — just choose her detail at checkout and it becomes hers.

The Reversible Pearl Lariat Necklace works as a standalone piece, but it's the kind of necklace that looks even better when you know it was chosen specifically for her. Same with bracelets and body chains — the extra thought translates.
Pieces That Work with Everything She Already Owns

The best gift jewelry bridges styles. It looks good on casual days and works for nights out. It doesn't demand a certain aesthetic — it just enhances whatever she's already wearing. That's why body chains, ankle chains, and delicate hand chains are such solid gifts. They're versatile in a way statement pieces often aren't.

A 2-in-1 Body Chain Necklace does double duty — belt or necklace depending on the day. The Boho Forehead Chain is subtle enough for everyday wear but special enough to make a moment feel intentional. The Boho Hair Chain is the kind of piece that works at a festival, at the beach, or just on a regular Tuesday when she feels like adding something extra. None of these require her to change her whole vibe — they just add to it.

Think about her style first. If she's minimal, go for something sleek and simple. If she's bohemian, lean into chains and layering. If she's maximalist, she'll love pieces that can be mixed and stacked. The right piece feels like an extension of who she already is, not a push in a new direction.

The best birthday gifts are the ones that disappear into everyday life because they fit so naturally. When it's something she'll actually reach for again and again, that's when you know you nailed it.

title: Gold vs Silver Body Jewelry: How to Choose
excerpt: The real difference between gold and silver jewelry—and which one actually works for your skin and style.

content.text: You're scrolling through body jewelry and you see it: the same piece in both gold and silver. So which one do you actually pick? It's not just about what looks pretty on the screen. The choice comes down to your skin tone, your existing jewelry, and honestly, how the metal feels against your skin.

Here's the thing—gold and silver are completely different metals, and they interact with your skin in different ways. Neither one is objectively "better." But one will almost always look better on you, and when you find it, you'll notice the difference immediately.
Does your skin tone matter?

Yes, but not in the way you think. It's less about whether you have warm or cool undertones and more about what you're already wearing. Look at your wrists right now. What color metal do you see on your existing rings, watches, or bracelets? That's your answer. Your jewelry should talk to each other, not fight.

If you're building a collection from scratch, gold tends to feel warmer and softer, while silver reads as cooler and more modern. Neither will look "wrong" on any skin tone—it's about personal preference and what makes you feel like yourself. Try holding both up to your wrist in natural light before you decide.
What about mixing gold and silver?

Mixing metals used to be considered a fashion rule-break. Now? It's completely normal. The trick is intentionality. If you're layering a Dainty Gold Body Chain with a silver belly chain, they should work together visually—not just happen to exist on your body at the same time.

The easiest way to make mixed metals work is to give them different jobs. Wear gold as your base layer and silver as an accent, or vice versa. Or keep them on different areas—a gold choker and silver anklets, for example. When metals have breathing room, they enhance each other instead of clashing.
What about your daily life and skin sensitivity?

Here's something people don't talk about enough: how the metal feels on your skin over time. All of our body jewelry is made from high-quality stainless steel that's waterproof and tarnish-resistant, so durability isn't the issue. What matters is whether you like the feeling of gold or silver against your body, especially if you're wearing it all day.

Some people find that one metal sits better against their skin or stays cooler or just feels more like "them." The only way to know is to try it. If you're ordering from us, keep track of which metal you reach for most. That's the one that works for you. Whether you're choosing a Turquoise Enamel Bead Double Choker or a Pearl Lariat Back Necklace, the metal should feel like an extension of you, not something you're constantly aware of.

So here's the real answer: pick the metal that matches what you're already wearing, that feels good on your skin, and that makes you want to put it on. That's not overthinking it—that's knowing yourself. The best jewelry is the piece you actually want to wear.

faq.question: Is gold or silver better for sensitive skin?
faq.answer: Both gold and silver stainless steel are hypoallergenic and gentle on sensitive skin—the material quality matters far more than the color. All Bodystrands jewelry is made from high-quality stainless steel that won't tarnish or cause irritation, so choose based on your personal preference and what other jewelry you own.

faq.question: Can you wear gold and silver jewelry together?
faq.answer: Yes, absolutely. Mixed metals look intentional and modern when you give them separate visual jobs—like pairing a gold body chain with silver anklets, or layering them on different areas of your body. The key is balance, not avoiding the combination.

faq.question: Which metal lasts longer, gold or silver?
faq.answer: With proper stainless steel construction, both last equally long and resist tarnishing. The durability depends on material quality, not the color—that's why Bodystrands pieces stay beautiful through daily wear, water, and time.

title: Layering Body Jewelry: The Art of Wearing More Without Looking Like Too Much
excerpt: Want to stack chains without the clutter? Here's how to layer body jewelry so it actually looks intentional.

content.text: There's a difference between wearing multiple pieces and wearing them well. Layering body jewelry isn't about throwing everything on at once—it's about creating a balanced look that feels like you, not a jewelry store explosion. The good news? It's easier than you think once you know the rules.

The key is restraint mixed with intention. You want pieces that work together, not compete. Think of layering like building an outfit—some parts take the spotlight, others play supporting roles. When you understand how to balance weight, texture, and placement, you can wear as much or as little as you want and it'll look deliberate.
Start with one statement piece

Pick the piece you actually want people to notice. Maybe it's a Thigh Chain with real presence, or a delicate Bridal Open-Back Necklace that sits perfectly on bare skin. This is your anchor. Everything else should support it, not fight for attention.

Once you've chosen your main piece, ask yourself: where is it worn? If it's bold and sits on your body, your secondary pieces should be thinner or more delicate. If it's already minimal, you have room to add layers. The math is simple—one loud voice, multiple whispers. Never two loud voices competing.

Your statement piece also tells you what metal to stick with. If you're wearing gold body jewelry, keep everything gold. If you're going silver or stainless steel, match that across the board. Mixing metals is fine if you're intentional, but matching creates instant cohesion.
Mix textures, not visual weight

This is where most people mess up. They layer three thick chains and wonder why it looks heavy. Instead, pair something chunky with something fine. A heavier piece can sit alongside delicate work—they balance each other. Try a Mirror Link Hand Chain with a thinner bracelet on the same wrist, or a bold body chain with minimal jewelry elsewhere.

Texture variety also keeps layering interesting. A smooth chain next to a linked or beaded piece creates visual depth without adding actual bulk. This is why mixing different styles from our body jewelry collection works so well—each piece has its own character, so even when worn together, nothing feels redundant.
The rule: if you're going bold on one body part, stay minimal everywhere else. Bold back chain? Keep your wrists simple. Stacked hand jewelry? Leave your neck bare. Let each layered moment breathe.
Spacing and placement matter more than you'd think

Two chains on your wrist aren't the same as two chains on your torso. Close proximity makes pieces feel clustered. When you're stacking on the same area (like a Multi-Strand Hand Chain with bracelets), the pieces should vary in width so they sit at slightly different levels and don't look like a solid block.

Spread your layers across your whole body instead of loading one zone. A chain here, a bracelet there, an anklet elsewhere. This gives you the effect of layering without the weight. Your eye moves across your body rather than getting stuck on one heavy area.

Think about negative space too. Bare skin is your friend when you're wearing multiple pieces. It keeps everything from feeling suffocating. A simple rule: if it starts to feel like armor, you've added too much.

faq.question: Can you wear two chains on the same part of your body?
faq.answer: Yes, but they should differ in weight or style so they sit at different levels and don't look like one solid mass. A delicate chain next to a bolder one works well—they complement rather than compete.

faq.question: How many pieces of body jewelry is too many?
faq.answer: There's no fixed number. It depends on whether your layering looks intentional or accidental. If each piece is visible and plays a role in your look, you're good. If things feel crowded or you're layering just to wear more, dial it back.

faq.question: Should all my body jewelry be the same metal?
faq.answer: Matching metals across all your pieces creates an effortless, cohesive look—it's the safest choice. Mixing metals can work beautifully, but only if you're doing it on purpose and spreading them out (not mixing them in the same stacked area).

title: How to Store Body Jewelry So It Stays Perfect
excerpt: The right storage keeps your chains and bracelets looking fresh for years. Here's exactly how to do it.

content.text: You've invested in pieces you love wearing. Whether it's a Double Shoulder Chest Chain or an everyday bracelet, proper storage is the difference between jewelry that lasts decades and jewelry that loses its shine. The good news: it doesn't require fancy solutions or complicated routines.

Most damage happens when pieces are tangled, exposed to moisture, or tossed randomly into a drawer. Our stainless steel body jewelry is built to resist tarnish and corrosion, but how you store it still matters. A few simple habits will keep your jewelry looking exactly like the day you got it.
Keep chains from tangling

Tangled chains are frustrating and can weaken the delicate links over time. The easiest fix is to store each piece separately or keep similar items grouped in their own small spaces. Use small pouches, a jewelry organizer with compartments, or even ziplock bags if you're traveling.

If you have multiple chains—like a Maximalist Layered Necklace Stack—lay them flat in a shallow box or drawer rather than coiling them. Some people hang delicate chains on a small hook or peg system, which prevents tangling while keeping pieces visible and accessible.
Store in a dry place away from moisture

Moisture is the enemy of any jewelry. Even though stainless steel resists tarnish far better than silver or gold, storing your pieces in a humid bathroom or damp closet still invites unnecessary damage. Keep your jewelry in a bedroom, living room, or anywhere with stable, dry conditions.

Avoid plastic bags for long-term storage—they trap moisture. Paper pouches or cotton cloth bags are better because they allow air to circulate. If you live somewhere particularly humid, silica gel packets in your jewelry box work wonders to absorb extra moisture and keep everything fresh.
A simple wooden jewelry box or ceramic dish on a shelf is often all you need. The key is keeping pieces away from bathrooms, kitchen splashes, and anywhere else where water or steam lingers.
Simple daily care extends storage life

Before you store a piece, wipe it down with a soft, dry cloth. This removes body oils, sweat, and any residue from your skin or clothing. You don't need anything fancy—a microfiber cloth or even a soft cotton t-shirt works. This one habit prevents buildup and keeps your chains and bracelets looking pristine.

If you wear a piece regularly—say, a Gemstone Zodiac Anklet all summer—occasional cleaning with warm soapy water and a soft toothbrush keeps it clean without damage. Dry it immediately and completely before storing. Store pieces you wear less frequently in the same dry, organized way, and they'll be ready whenever you reach for them again.

faq.question: Can I store body jewelry in the bathroom?
faq.answer: No. Bathrooms are humid, and moisture damages jewelry over time. Store your pieces in a dry bedroom, closet, or living area instead. If you need quick access after showering, wait until pieces are completely dry before putting them away.

faq.question: What's the best way to prevent chain tangles?
faq.answer: Store each chain separately in its own pouch, compartment, or small box. If you have multiple chains, lay them flat rather than coiling them. Avoid hanging too many pieces together on one hook.

faq.question: Should I clean my jewelry before storing it?
faq.answer: Yes. Wipe each piece with a soft, dry cloth before storing to remove body oils and sweat. For pieces you wear regularly, rinse with warm soapy water and a soft toothbrush, then dry completely before storing away.

title: Layer Jewelry Over Sweaters: What Actually Works

Your shoulder chain just... disappears under a chunky turtleneck. The good news? You don't have to choose between comfort and looking put-together. You just need to know what pieces actually work over knitwear.
The secret is choosing jewelry that's intentional about visibility and designed to sit *on* your sweater, not get swallowed by it. Think layered, think bold, think strategic.
Long necklaces and stacked layers

This is where sweater season actually works in your favor. Long necklaces that would look weird over bare skin suddenly make sense layered over a crewneck or v-neck. They sit on top of the fabric and catch the light without getting tangled up.

Stack them. A longer chain underneath with a shorter one on top creates visual interest and makes sure both pieces stay visible. The Turquoise & Zodiac Necklace Stack is built for exactly this—two pieces that work together, not against each other. Pair it with a simple crew neck sweater and suddenly you have dimension without chaos.

The trick is avoiding necklaces that cling to your neck or disappear into the neckline. You want pieces with enough length to sit visibly on the sweater's surface. If it's meant to sit at collarbone height, it'll get lost. If it's meant to reach chest or lower, you're golden.
Chains that go *over* your sweater

Back chains, shoulder chains, and body chains are the real MVPs of sweater season. They're designed to sit on top of your outfit, which means sweaters are actually the perfect canvas. A back chain adds structure and dimension. A shoulder chain draws the eye upward and elongates. These aren't hidden—they're featured.

Wear them over fitted sweaters, oversized sweaters, cardigans, and even sweater dresses. They work because they're meant to be seen. Unlike a delicate bracelet that gets swallowed by a sleeve, chains that cross your back or drape your shoulders are made to be noticed. The fabric becomes part of the aesthetic, not a barrier.
Bracelets and hand chains that don't catch

Bracelets are tricky over sweaters because long sleeves can catch and pull. The solution? Hand chains and finger chains, which sit higher on your hand and don't interact with your sleeve at all. Or go for a bracelet and wear it over your sweater cuff—let it sit on top of the fabric instead of tucked underneath.

The Boho Finger Hand Chain is perfect for this. It reaches across your hand and between your fingers, so it stays in place whether your sleeves are long or short. No snagging. No shifting. Just clean, visible jewelry that complements rather than competes with your knit.

All of our pieces are handmade from high-quality stainless steel, so they're built to handle everyday wear—including sweater season snags and texture shifts. They won't tarnish, they won't discolor, and they won't break under the friction of fabric.

The real rule? Visible and intentional beats hidden and delicate every single time. Pick pieces that *want* to sit on top of your sweater, layer them thoughtfully, and let the jewelry do what it's supposed to do—make you feel like yourself, even when you're wrapped in knitwear.

title: Layering Necklaces at Different Lengths (The Right Way)
excerpt: Master the art of stacking necklaces so they actually look intentional instead of tangled.

content.text: Layered necklaces can look effortless and intentional—or they can look like an accident. The difference comes down to one thing: length. Get the spacing right, and suddenly you have a look that feels polished and personal. Get it wrong, and everything tangles together into a confused mess around your collarbone.
The good news? There's a simple formula, and once you know it, you'll never second-guess yourself again.
The three-necklace rule

Start with a short choker or collar piece—something that sits high on your neck, anywhere from 14 to 18 inches. This is your anchor. A delicate choker works beautifully here because it frames your face without demanding attention.

Next, add a mid-length necklace around 20 to 24 inches. This should sit just below your collarbone and create visual separation from the choker. This is where you can go bolder—try something with texture or a small pendant. The Star Pendant Rhinestone Choker sits in this sweet spot and adds just enough sparkle to break up the layers.

Finally, layer a longer piece at 28 inches or beyond. This should reach your sternum or lower and acts as the statement layer. The length creates breathing room, so even if you choose something ornate, the overall effect feels curated rather than crowded.
When two necklaces are enough

Not every outfit needs three layers. Two necklaces at contrasting lengths can be more striking than a full stack. Pair a short choker with something that drops well past your collarbone—at least 8 inches of separation between where they sit on your body.

This is actually the easiest way to start experimenting with layering. You'll quickly get a feel for what spacing looks right on your frame. Try a Colorful Crystal Bead Choker paired with a longer chain, and you'll see how the contrast makes both pieces shine.
What actually works with different necklines

A high crew neck or turtleneck eats up space, so skip the choker and start with your mid-length piece instead. You need room to breathe, literally. Layering on top of a bulky neckline just creates visual clutter.

Low necklines and scoop necks are your playground—this is where longer layers shine. You've got the real estate to work with, so go ahead and stack. A plunging v-neck can handle three full layers without looking cramped.

Boat necks and off-shoulders are trickier. Your collarbone is exposed but in a sideways direction, so layering works best when you keep pieces closer together and avoid anything that slides too far to one side.
The key: your necklaces should follow the natural line of your neckline, not fight against it. Once you have the lengths right, the rest falls into place—literally.

faq.question: What length should my first choker be when layering necklaces?
faq.answer: Your first choker should sit high on your neck between 14 to 18 inches, depending on your neck size and how close to the skin you want it. This is your anchor, so it should feel snug but not tight—you want it to frame your face, not choke you.

faq.question: How much space should there be between layered necklaces?
faq.answer: Aim for at least 2 to 4 inches of visible space between where each necklace sits on your chest. This prevents them from tangling and makes each piece feel intentional rather than accidental. A simple way to check: if you can't slide a finger between the layers, they're too close.

faq.question: Can you layer more than three necklaces?

Stick with three unless you're going for a specific bold aesthetic—and even then, make sure each piece has breathing room.

title: Gold Plated vs Gold Tone: What Actually Lasts Longer
excerpt: One sounds fancier, but they're completely different. Here's what you need to know before buying.

content.text: You've probably seen both terms thrown around when shopping for jewelry. Gold plated. Gold tone. They sound similar enough that you might think they're the same thing with different marketing. They're not. Understanding the difference matters because it directly affects how long your jewelry lasts and how it ages.

Let's cut through the confusion. We make body jewelry that's meant to be worn every day — in the shower, at the beach, through life. So we've thought a lot about durability. Here's what actually separates these two.
What gold plated actually means

Gold plating is a real process. A thin layer of actual gold is bonded to a base metal underneath — usually stainless steel or brass. That gold layer is typically between 0.5 to 2.5 microns thick. It's real gold sitting on top of something else.

The catch? That thin gold layer wears away over time. Friction, sweat, soap, chlorine — they all speed up the process. You might get 6-18 months of regular wear before the plating starts to fade or chip. After that, you're seeing the base metal underneath, and the magic is gone. Gold plating isn't repairable on handmade pieces like ours, so once it wears, it's done.
What gold tone actually is

Gold tone is just stainless steel (or another metal) that's been colored or finished to look gold. No actual gold involved. It's painted on, basically. Think of it like the difference between a gold-painted wall and a wall covered in gold leaf.

Here's the real advantage: gold tone doesn't chip or peel the way plating does. The color is part of the metal itself. It can fade or dull slightly over years of wear, but it doesn't suddenly reveal a completely different metal underneath. You get more consistent wear, even if the shine dulls eventually.

We work exclusively with high-quality stainless steel that's waterproof and tarnish-resistant. It's built to handle daily life — showers, sweat, salt water, everything. Browse our full shop all body jewelry collection and you'll notice we don't do gold plating. We chose durability over that initial gleam.
Which one should you actually choose

If you love the look of gold and want something you can wear constantly without thinking about maintenance, gold tone is the smarter choice. It lasts longer without the heartbreak of watching it peel. If you want actual gold on your skin and don't mind replacing a piece every year or so, gold plating works — just go in knowing the timeline.

The pieces we make — like our Birthstone Ring — are designed to be part of your everyday. You wear them to the beach. You shower in them. You sleep in them. That's why we built them to last without the fuss of gold plating wearing away. Real materials, real durability, no surprises.

faq.question: Is gold plated jewelry real gold?
faq.answer: Yes, the outer layer is real gold, but it's extremely thin (less than 3 microns). The base underneath is a different metal, usually stainless steel or brass. Over time with regular wear, that thin gold layer wears away and exposes the base metal beneath it.

faq.question: How long does gold plated jewelry last?
faq.answer: With regular wear, gold plating typically lasts 6-18 months before you start seeing fading or chipping. The timeline depends on how often you wear it, whether you expose it to water and sweat, and the thickness of the plating. Heavy daily wear speeds up the process significantly.

faq.question: Does gold tone jewelry fade?
faq.answer: Gold tone can fade or dull slightly over years of heavy wear because the color is a surface finish, not the material itself. However, it won't chip or peel the way plating does — it degrades gradually rather than suddenly revealing a different metal underneath.

title: Style Shoulder Chains for Autumn: The Easy Guide
excerpt: Shoulder chains aren't just for summer. Here's how to layer them into your autumn wardrobe without overthinking it.

content.text: Shoulder chains feel like a summer thing, right? But autumn is actually when they shine. You've got more fabric to play with — sweaters, cardigans, jackets — which means more ways to make a chain work. The key is layering them intentionally so they sit on top of what you're wearing, not hidden under it.

The good news: you probably don't need new chains. Your summer pieces will work just fine. You just need to think about how they sit against your autumn fabrics and what neckline you're pairing them with.
Pairing chains with necklines that actually show them

The biggest mistake people make in autumn is burying their chains under crew necks and turtlenecks. If you want your chain visible, wear it over a scoop neck, V-neck, or open button-up. Those necklines create negative space where your chain can actually live.

Cardigans are your secret weapon here. Throw one open over a simple tee or tank and let your chain sit on top of both layers. You get the warmth of autumn dressing without hiding the jewelry. Shop all shoulder chains to find pieces that complement your existing sweater rotation.
If you're a turtleneck person, that's fine — just wear your chain over the turtleneck instead of under it. It creates a layered look that feels intentional, not accidental.
Choosing metals and styles that match autumn colors

Stainless steel chains work with everything because they don't tarnish or react to what you wear them against. That means you can pair the same chain with burgundy one day and mustard yellow the next without worrying about it looking weird against your skin tone.

When autumn means jewel tones and earth tones, thinner chains often feel lighter and less heavy against sweaters. A delicate chain won't compete with a chunky knit. If you're wearing something minimal — a slip dress under a blazer, say — that's when a chunkier chain makes sense and actually becomes the focal point.
Think about texture too. A matte finish chain reads differently against a smooth silk camisole versus a fuzzy wool sweater. Both work, but the contrast changes the whole vibe.
Layering chains without the mess

Two chains are better than one, but only if they actually sit right. In autumn, when you're wearing thicker fabrics, chains can shift around more. Make sure they're long enough to sit properly on your shoulders — not too tight, not so loose they slide off when you move.

If you're layering multiple chains, vary the lengths slightly. One at the collarbone, one lower. This keeps things from tangling and makes the look feel deliberate. And if you're wearing a jacket or blazer, wear your chains on top of it for maximum visibility — otherwise, what's the point?

Autumn dressing doesn't mean your body jewelry disappears. It just means being a little more intentional about where it sits and what it sits on. Keep it simple, keep it visible, and your chains will look just as good in October as they did in July.

faq.question: Can you wear shoulder chains under sweaters in autumn?
faq.answer: You can, but it defeats the purpose — your chain will be hidden and could shift around under the fabric. Instead, wear it over an open cardigan, scoop neck, or button-up so it actually shows.

faq.question: Do shoulder chains work with cardigans?

faq.question: What length shoulder chain is best for autumn outfits?

title: Mix Gold and Silver Jewelry Without the Doubt
excerpt: Stop letting the "no mixing metals" rule stop you. Here's exactly how to wear gold and silver together.

content.text: You've probably heard it before: gold and silver don't mix. But that rule is outdated, and honestly? It was never really a rule at all. The truth is simpler than you think — mixing metals is about intention, not restriction. Your wrists and neck can absolutely handle both, and when you do it right, they look better for it.

The key isn't to avoid one metal or stick rigidly to one tone. It's to think about balance and what actually works with your skin. Once you understand that, you'll feel confident wearing whatever combination feels right to you.
Start with your skin tone

Your skin naturally leans warm or cool, and that's the foundation for mixing metals confidently. If you have warm undertones (golden, peachy), gold will feel more natural next to your skin — but silver can still work beautifully as an accent. If you're cool-toned (pink, red undertones), silver tends to feel closer to your natural palette, but gold adds warmth and interest.

The thing is: you don't have to choose just one. Cool-toned skin can absolutely wear gold. Warm-toned skin looks amazing in silver. The difference is in how you balance them. Think of it like wearing outfits — you're creating harmony, not following a rigid dress code.
The balance rule: lead with one, accent with the other

Here's the practical framework that makes mixing metals actually easy. Pick one metal as your main player — the one that dominates your look. That's usually your watch, your go-to necklace, or your main bracelet. Let that metal be 60-70% of what you're wearing. Then, use the second metal in smaller, secondary pieces. One delicate accent piece. One thin chain. One charm or detail.

For example: wear a gold Goddess Shoulder Chain as your statement piece, then add a silver Dainty Summer Belly Chain underneath. The gold leads; the silver whispers. No conflict. No confusion. Just intention.

This approach works everywhere — your hands, your neck, your body. One metal takes the spotlight. The other adds depth. When you have that visual hierarchy, your eye sees a complete look instead of a clash.
Where to layer without overthinking it

Layering is where people get most nervous about mixing metals, but it's actually one of the easiest places to do it. Wear your gold necklace at your collarbone, then layer a thinner silver chain below it. The different lengths keep them visually separate, so mixing metals becomes an asset instead of a worry. Each chain gets its own space.

The same works for your wrists and body. A gold bracelet with a silver body chain doesn't compete — they occupy different visual zones. Stack a Pearl Lariat Back Necklace in silver with gold body jewelry, and suddenly the mix feels intentional and balanced instead of accidental.

The real freedom here? You get to build layers that actually feel like you, not layers that follow some invisible rulebook. Mix metals the way you mix your outfits — with confidence and your own taste as the guide.

faq.question: Can you actually wear gold and silver together?
faq.answer: Yes, completely. The outdated rule against mixing metals was never based on anything real. Gold and silver worn together look intentional and modern — as long as you balance them so one metal leads and the other plays a supporting role.

faq.question: What skin tone looks better in gold or silver?

title: Transition Your Jewelry into Fall: A Styling Guide

The trick isn't swapping everything out — it's layering smarter, choosing metals that work harder, and pairing delicate chains with pieces that ground them in the season. The best part? Body jewelry is built for this. Stainless steel pieces work year-round without tarnishing or losing their shine, so your summer favorites stay as strong in October as they were in July. The transition is purely about how you wear them.
Layer chains with intention, not clutter

Summer layering was all air and negative space. Fall layering is about creating intentional texture. Where you might have worn a single delicate belly chain over bare skin in August, now you're layering it under a fitted sweater or pairing it with a longer cardigan. Choose metals and accents that echo fall tones

Your silver and stainless steel chains don't need to change, but what you wear them with should shift. In summer, you paired them with gold accents, pastels, and bright metals. As fall arrives, introduce deeper tones — burgundy, olive, rust, charcoal, cream. Your chain doesn't need to match these colors; it just needs to sit comfortably against them.

If you own personalized pieces like a Monogram Letter Necklace, fall is when they really shine. Initials feel more grounded against darker, heavier fabrics. They also pair beautifully with layered necklaces — wear your monogram with a longer chain underneath for added depth without looking busy.

You're not replacing your summer jewelry — you're repositioning it.

The transition from summer to fall jewelry isn't about buying new pieces. It's about wearing what you already own in ways that match the season. Your chains work in September just as well as they did in June. The only thing that needs to change is how you style them.

title: Gold Plated vs Gold Tone: What You Actually Need to Know
excerpt: One lasts years. One won't. Here's how to tell the difference—and which one's actually worth your money.

content.text: You're scrolling through jewelry and you see two pieces that look identical. One says "gold plated." The other says "gold tone." They cost different amounts. You have no idea which one to pick. If that sounds familiar, you're not alone—and the difference between these two terms matters way more than most people realize.

Here's the thing: these aren't just different words for the same thing. One is an actual layer of real gold. The other is basically paint. Knowing which is which will save you from buying jewelry that tarnishes in three months or investing in something that'll actually last.
What gold plated actually is

Gold plating is a real process. A thin layer of genuine gold is bonded to a base metal (usually copper or brass) using electricity. That layer is typically between 0.5 to 2.5 microns thick—thin enough that it costs way less than solid gold, but thick enough to actually be gold.

The upside: it looks like real gold and it'll stay that way for a while. How long? If you take care of it—avoid constant water, sweat, and friction—a quality gold-plated piece can last 1-3 years. Some last longer. Eventually, the layer wears through and you'll see the base metal underneath, but you get real value out of it first.
What gold tone is (and why it's different)

Gold tone is just a description. It means the metal is colored or painted to look gold. There's no actual gold in the plating process—just a coating applied to make it gold-colored. It's cheaper, faster, and it shows.

Here's the reality: gold tone jewelry will tarnish, fade, and chip much faster. We're talking months, not years. Once it starts to wear, it peels, flakes, or discolors unevenly. And there's no "real gold" underneath—just base metal that will eventually oxidize or discolor.
This doesn't mean gold tone is always a bad choice. If you want something fun and temporary for €15, go for it. But if you're looking for jewelry you'll actually wear regularly, it's not the move.
Why we skip both—and what we do instead

At Bodystrands, we don't do gold plating or gold tone. We work with high-quality stainless steel instead. It's waterproof, it doesn't tarnish, and it genuinely lasts through everyday wear—swimming, showers, gym sessions, all of it.

Stainless steel has a bright, clean aesthetic that works with almost any look. It's different from gold, sure, but it's honest about what it is. You get a piece that's built to last, made by hand in our Portuguese studio, at prices that won't hurt your wallet. Whether you're drawn to something like our Monogram Letter Necklace or exploring our full body jewelry collection, you know exactly what you're getting and how long it'll actually stick around.

The real difference between gold plated and gold tone comes down to this: one is real gold (that'll eventually wear off), one is fake gold (that'll fall apart faster). Neither needs to be your only option. Pick the material that matches how you actually live—and wear your jewelry without worrying.

faq.question: Does gold tone jewelry tarnish?
faq.answer: Yes. Gold tone is a coating designed to look gold, but it has no actual gold in it. It tarnishes, fades, and chips much faster than gold-plated jewelry—usually within months of regular wear.

faq.question: How long does gold plated jewelry last?
faq.answer: A well-made gold-plated piece typically lasts 1-3 years with regular wear, depending on how often you expose it to water, sweat, and friction. The gold layer gradually wears through and reveals the base metal underneath.

faq.question: Is gold tone or gold plated better?
faq.answer: Gold plated is better if you want jewelry that lasts. It has actual gold bonded to the base metal, so it looks and wears like real gold for much longer than gold tone, which is just a color coating that chips and fades quickly.

title: Why Stainless Steel Is Best for Jewelry You Wear Every Day

What makes stainless steel different from regular metal

Regular steel rusts. It oxidizes. Stainless steel has chromium mixed into it, and that chromium creates an invisible protective layer on the surface. When oxygen touches it, that layer reforms automatically. It's not magic — it's chemistry that actually works.

Because of that layer, stainless steel doesn't tarnish the way silver does. It won't corrode from sweat, saltwater, or chlorine. You can wear a Dragonfly Charm Belly Chain to the beach, dive in, and it'll look the same when you get out. That's the real-world difference.
Why waterproof and tarnish-resistant matter for your lifestyle

Think about what you actually do. You shower with your jewelry on. You swim. You work out. You sleep in it sometimes. With stainless steel, you don't have to think about it. No special cleaning rituals. No taking it off before bed. No stress about damage.

Other materials need babying. Gold needs to be polished regularly. Silver tarnishes and needs constant attention. Plated jewelry wears through and exposes base metal underneath. Stainless steel just sits there, solid and unchanged. That's what makes it built for everyday wear — and why we chose it for every piece we make, from our full body jewelry collection to smaller pieces like bracelets and necklaces.
If you have sensitive skin, stainless steel is also a safer bet than lower-quality metals. It's non-reactive and won't irritate most people. You get durability and comfort in one material.
How quality stainless steel stays looking new

The best part? It doesn't fade, dull, or change color over time. A piece like our Pink Cross Choker Necklace looks as bright in year two as it did on day one. That's not marketing — that's the material itself.

Occasionally you might see a tiny water spot or dust on the surface, but that wipes clean instantly. There's no hidden damage happening underneath. With stainless steel, what you see is what you get, and what you get lasts.

title: Layering Jewelry Over Long Sleeves: Make It Visible
excerpt: Your favorite chains don't have to disappear under winter knitwear. Here's how to layer them so they actually show.

content.text: Long sleeves are great until they swallow your jewelry whole. You spent time choosing the perfect piece, and now it's hidden under a sweater. The good news: you don't have to choose between warmth and showing off what you love. It just takes a little strategy.
Layering jewelry over sleeves isn't about fighting fabric—it's about working with it. The key is understanding which pieces sit where, which fabrics cooperate, and a few tricks that actually work.
Choose fabrics that play nice with chains

Not all long sleeves are created equal. Thin, smooth fabrics like silk blends, cotton jersey, and fitted knits work best because chains sit on top instead of sinking in. Chunky knits and textured fabrics grab at your jewelry and make everything slide around—avoid those if visibility is your goal.

Fitted sleeves matter more than you'd think. A slim-fitting long-sleeve top or fitted tee under a loose sweater gives you a solid base for chains to rest on. Oversized sleeves create too much fabric, and your jewelry either disappears or keeps shifting.

Pro tip: layer a thin long-sleeve base under a short-sleeve piece or sleeveless top. You get the warmth without the bulk, and your chains have a smooth surface to sit on. A Silver Shoulder Harness looks incredible this way—the structure stays visible and sits exactly where you want it.
Strategic piece placement for layered looks

Where your jewelry sits matters. Shoulder and neck pieces work best over long sleeves because they're naturally positioned to rest on top. Arm chains and hand chains need more careful styling—they tend to ride up or get covered unless you're intentional.

If you're wearing a Birthstone Thigh Chain or Double Drape Thigh Chain, you're already ahead—those sit high enough that long sleeves won't touch them at all. For wrists and forearms, consider wearing pieces slightly higher than usual, or pair them with pushed-up sleeves so they actually show.
Layering multiple chains? Start with simpler pieces closest to your skin, then add bolder statement pieces on the outside. This gives dimension and makes sure nothing gets buried.
The sleeve roll and the open cardigan move

Sometimes the simplest solution works best. Rolling your sleeves up past your wrists or elbows instantly reveals any arm, wrist, or hand chains. It also looks intentional and chic—not like you forgot to pull your sleeves down.

An open cardigan or shirt jacket over your layers is another game-changer. You stay warm, sleeves are visible and positioned away from your skin, and your jewelry gets full attention. A Pearl Glasses Chain or necklace is stunning under an open layered look like this.

You can also wear loose sleeves pushed to your forearms or intentionally slide them up and down throughout the day. It's dynamic, it keeps your pieces visible, and it looks way more deliberate than accidentally covered jewelry.

The truth is, your body jewelry is made to be worn and seen—not to hide. Winter layering doesn't have to mean sacrificing the pieces you love. Pick your fabrics smart, position your pieces intentionally, and don't be afraid to adjust as you go. That's real styling.

faq.answer: Yes, but they work best on thin, fitted sleeves that don't bunch up. Oversized or textured sleeves tend to cover or shift the chains. Pushing your sleeves up slightly or wearing them on top of a fitted base layer makes arm chains visible and keeps them in place.

title: Layer Necklaces Like You Mean It: A Length Guide
excerpt: Layering necklaces is easy once you know the spacing rules. Here's exactly how to do it right.

content.text: Layering necklaces isn't random. The difference between "wow, that looks intentional" and "did she get dressed in the dark" comes down to one thing: spacing. When you know the right distances between chains, suddenly everything clicks into place. You don't need to overthink it—just follow the basic rules and your neck will look like you actually planned this.
The good news? You probably already own most of what you need to layer well. The bad news? Most people space their chains way too close together. Let's fix that.
The Standard Lengths That Actually Work

Layering works because different lengths sit at different parts of your collarbone and chest. A choker sits flush against your neck (usually 14-16 inches). A princess length hits just at your collarbone (18 inches). A matinee hangs mid-chest (20-24 inches). A opera goes lower (28-34 inches). When you pick three pieces at these different lengths, they naturally space themselves without looking cramped.

The key is leaving real distance between each layer. If two chains are only an inch apart, they blur together and look accidental. When you have at least 2-3 inches between each one, your eye can see each piece separately. Try pairing a choker with a matinee length, then add an opera piece. That's three distinct levels, three distinct looks, one cohesive stack. Something like our Cross & Zodiac Necklace Stack does this math for you—each chain lands at a different sweet spot.
How to Mix Styles Without Clashing

Mixing delicate chains with bolder pieces is where layering gets interesting. The rule is simple: let the bolder piece breathe. If you're wearing a chunky cross pendant at your chest, don't put another chunky piece right next to it. Instead, pair it with something minimal—a thin gold chain or a simple pearl strand above and below it.

Think about your metals too. Stainless steel works with literally everything, which is why our whole collection is built on it—no tarnish, no drama, just clean layering that lasts. You can mix different pendant styles without worrying about one chain oxidizing before the other. A Rosary Pearl Cross Choker pairs beautifully with something simpler underneath it because the pearls and cross draw attention, while a minimal strand supports without competing.
Don't match everything. Intentional mixing looks better than perfect matching. One sparkly strand, one minimal strand, one textured piece. That contrast is what makes people notice the whole look.
Building Your Layering Starter Kit

You don't need many pieces to layer well. Start with one choker, one mid-length chain, and one longer piece. All three should be materials and styles you actually wear. If you hate rose gold, don't buy rose gold just because it's trendy. The best layered look is one you'll actually put on.

Build from there. Add personality with pendants—birthstones, initials, zodiac signs, whatever speaks to you. Our necklaces collection includes pieces designed specifically for layering, so you're not hunting through random options. Most pieces are under €40, which means you can experiment without spending a fortune. The high-quality stainless steel means whatever you choose will handle daily wear without degrading or tarnishing.
Once you nail the spacing and let each chain have its moment, you'll stop thinking about whether it looks right. It just will.

faq.question: What's the ideal distance between layered necklaces?
faq.answer: Aim for at least 2-3 inches between each chain. This creates visible separation so each layer reads as its own piece rather than a tangled mess. If your chains are too close, they blur together visually.

faq.question: Can you layer necklaces with different metals?
faq.answer: Yes, absolutely. Stainless steel mixes beautifully with gold, silver, rose gold, and other metals because it's neutral enough to complement rather than compete. The key is intentional spacing, not metal matching.

title: How to Store Body Jewelry So It Actually Lasts
excerpt: Keep your chains looking brand new. Here's exactly how to store them—no complicated steps needed.

content.text: You invested in a piece you love. Maybe it's a Script Initial Bracelet with your initial, or a Zodiac Belly Chain that actually means something to you. So it makes sense to keep it looking as good as the day it arrived. The good news: storing body jewelry properly isn't hard. It just takes a few intentional habits.

All of our pieces are made from high-quality stainless steel, which means they're built to handle everyday wear, water, and sweat without tarnishing or corroding. That durability is real. But storage still matters. How you keep your jewelry when you're not wearing it determines whether it stays pristine or starts to look dull or tangled.
The basics: dry, cool, away from humidity

Start with the fundamentals. Store your jewelry in a cool, dry place—a bedroom drawer is ideal. Moisture and humidity are the biggest threats to any metal, even stainless steel. If you live somewhere humid or you like to keep jewelry in a bathroom, rethink it. Condensation builds up over time, and that's when you'll start seeing things you don't want to see.

Keep pieces away from direct sunlight, extreme heat, and temperature swings. Don't store them near a radiator, heater, or windowsill where the sun hits all day. Stable conditions mean stable jewelry. Simple as that.

If you're storing multiple pieces together, make sure they're not in a pile or tangled in a box. Chains, especially longer ones like Bridal Hair Vine Chains, can get knotted around each other. That doesn't damage them, but it's annoying to untangle.
Keep them separated and organized

The easiest method is to use small pouches, compartments, or even ziplock bags—one piece per bag. This prevents tangling, keeps dust off, and makes it easy to grab exactly what you want. You don't need anything fancy. A fabric jewelry box with dividers works. So does a drawer organizer with small sections.

If you wear pieces regularly—like a Pearl Glasses Chain or a daily bracelet—keep it somewhere visible and easy to reach instead of buried. The more accessible something is, the more likely you'll actually wear it instead of letting it sit forgotten.

For delicate or sentimental pieces, consider a small box or padded pouch that you keep in a drawer or shelf. These are the pieces you're saving or wearing for special occasions. They deserve a little extra care.
Before you store it: clean and dry

Always clean your jewelry before storing it, especially if you've been wearing it all day or after swimming or working out. Sweat, salt water, and chlorine can leave residue that builds up over time. A quick rinse under lukewarm water and a gentle dry with a soft cloth is all you need. Make sure it's completely dry before putting it away—no moisture lingering.

If there's visible buildup or it just needs a deeper clean, use a soft toothbrush or microfiber cloth. You're not doing anything aggressive here. Stainless steel is tough, but gentle handling keeps everything looking its best. Once it's dry, it's ready to go in its storage spot.

That's really it. Dry storage, separated pieces, stable temperature, and a quick clean before you put things away. Your jewelry will stay looking new, won't tangle, and will be ready to wear whenever you want it. El and Gio make each piece by hand for you—treating it right means it'll last.

faq.question: Is it okay to store stainless steel jewelry in a ziplock bag?
faq.answer: Yes, absolutely. A ziplock bag is one of the best storage methods because it keeps moisture and dust away, prevents tangling, and is super affordable. Just make sure the jewelry is completely dry before you seal it.

faq.question: Can I store my body jewelry in a humid bathroom?
faq.answer: It's better to avoid it. Even though stainless steel resists tarnishing, constant humidity can cause slight discoloration or dullness over time. A cool, dry bedroom or closet is ideal.

faq.question: How often should I clean my jewelry before storing it?
faq.answer: Clean it before storing it if you've worn it daily, been sweating, or exposed it to saltwater or chlorine. For pieces you wear occasionally, a quick rinse and dry is fine. Just make sure nothing is wet when it goes in storage.

title: What Is a Birthstone Bracelet and Which One Should You Choose

The 12 birthstones and what each month represents

July is ruby (red, for passion). August is peridot (yellow-green, for healing). September is sapphire (blue, for wisdom). October splits between opal and tourmaline (both protective). The meanings matter if you want them to, but here's the real thing: you don't need to believe in the symbolism for a birthstone bracelet to feel meaningful. Sometimes you just like how the stone looks, and that's enough.

Start with your birth month. That's the foundation. But then ask yourself what you actually want to wear — do you prefer cool tones or warm ones? Sparkle or soft? Something delicate or something that makes a statement? Your birthstone should align with your style, not fight it.

Think about the setting too. A birthstone can be a single focal point, part of a charm bracelet, or layered with other stones. The Pearl Charm Bracelet works beautifully if you want something understated. The Layered Turquoise Bead Bracelet is perfect if you like texture and depth. Your wrist should feel like it's wearing *you*, not the other way around.

Consider who might wear it too. Gifting someone their birthstone bracelet is meaningful because it says you know them. It's personal without being heavy-handed. If you're shopping for yourself, you get to be selfish — pick what makes you feel good every time you look down.

All of our bracelets are made from high-quality stainless steel, so your birthstone bracelet won't tarnish or fade, no matter how much you wear it. That means you can actually live in it, day and night, through showers and swims. It's built to be part of your life, not something you save for special occasions.
Make it yours

The beauty of a birthstone bracelet is how personal it can be. You customize it at checkout — choose your birth month, and the bracelet shows up made exactly for you. No factory production line, no compromise. It's handmade by us, El and Gio, right here in our Portuguese studio.

Whether you're buying for yourself or someone else, a birthstone bracelet is one of those pieces that sits right at the intersection of meaningful and wearable. It's jewelry that tells a small story every single time you put it on.

title: Build a Year-Round Jewelry Wardrobe (Without Overthinking It)

Add personalization that matters to you

This is where your wardrobe actually becomes yours. Personalized pieces — whether it's your birthstone, birth flower, zodiac sign, or initial — give you something no one else has. They're not fussy. They're subtle details that you notice and that matter to you.

A Birth Flower Anklet works the same way in spring as it does in winter. You wear the same piece year-round because it's genuinely *yours*. Same with a Birthstone Thigh Chain — it's tied to something real about who you are, not a trend that'll fade by next season.

This approach means fewer pieces do more work. You're not buying a separate wardrobe for December. You're just thinking differently about what you already own.

title: How to Wear an Eyeglasses Chain Without Looking Accidental
excerpt: An eyeglasses chain can look intentional and styled—here's exactly how to do it.

content.text: An eyeglasses chain used to signal one thing: you needed your glasses to stay put. Now it signals something else entirely—that you know how to layer, you have a sense of humor about function meeting fashion, and you're not afraid to wear something useful as jewelry. The trick is making it look like you chose it deliberately. And you did. Here's how to wear it that way.

The baseline: pick a chain that actually fits your style. If you dress minimal, a simple silver chain works. If you lean boho, go beaded. The chain should feel like an extension of what you already wear, not something tacked on.
Anchor it to what you're already wearing

The easiest way to make an eyeglasses chain look intentional is to match it to your other jewelry. If you wear gold, pick gold. If you're all silver and pearls, go that direction. Your chain should whisper "part of the plan," not "oh, I also grabbed this."

Think about the vibe of your other pieces too. A delicate Pearl Glasses Chain pairs naturally with minimalist earrings and a simple necklace. A Boho Beaded Eyeglasses Chain sits better alongside textured bracelets and layered necklaces. You're not trying to match exactly—you're trying to tell a coherent story with your jewelry.
Wear your glasses intentionally (not just when you need them)

Here's the honest truth: your chain only looks intentional if your glasses do. If you're pushing them up your head or taking them on and off constantly, the chain reads as functional, not styled. Wear your glasses on your face, the way you'd wear any other accessory.

That means picking frames you actually like looking at. Oversized frames, cat-eyes, thin metal rims—these read as style choices. A beat-up pair you grab out of desperation does not. If you're investing in a chain, you're signaling that your glasses are part of your look. Own it.

And yes, this works even if you don't need glasses every day. Some of the best-styled chains belong to people who wear glasses sometimes, for the way they look. There's no rule that says a glasses chain has to serve a practical purpose. If it looks good, it works.
Choose a chain length that sits naturally

Length matters more than most people think. Too long and it looks like it's floating. Too short and it feels restrictive. A well-fitted chain should rest around your collarbone when your glasses are on—long enough to feel comfortable, short enough that it doesn't disappear into your shirt.

The best chains work in a range, so you can adjust based on your neckline and what you're wearing. A simple Eyeglasses Chain in high-quality stainless steel gives you flexibility and durability without the fuss. And since it's waterproof and tarnish-resistant, you can actually wear it every day without worrying about it looking dull or worn.

There's no such thing as an accident with the right chain. Pick one that fits your style, wear your glasses on purpose, and let the chain do what it's designed to do—make sure they stay put, and look good while it happens.

title: How to Mix Gold and Silver Jewelry Without It Looking Chaotic
excerpt: The rule isn't no mixing—it's knowing how to do it right. Here's exactly how.

content.text: You've probably heard that gold and silver don't go together. That's outdated advice. The truth is simpler: mixing metals is fine—you just need intention. When you mix gold and silver thoughtfully, you look intentional instead of accidental. Here's how to do it.
Start with one dominant metal

Pick which metal you want to lead. If you're wearing mostly silver pieces, add just one or two gold accents. If gold is your base, let silver play a supporting role. This isn't a hard rule—it's a visual anchor that keeps the mix from feeling scattered.

Think of it like outfit proportions. You wouldn't wear equal amounts of two competing colors, right? Same logic applies here. Your dominant metal should show up in your core pieces—maybe a necklace or body chain—while the other metal appears in smaller doses like a bracelet or anklet.
For example, a Reversible Pearl Lariat Necklace in silver can be your statement piece, then layer in a smaller gold bracelet or ring. The asymmetry feels natural, not confusing.
Use texture and style as your real guide

Here's the actual secret: metal tone matters far less than whether your pieces look intentional together. Delicate chains mix easily with chunky chains. Boho-style pieces work with minimalist ones if you're deliberate. The visual weight and vibe matter more than the color.

A sleek Initial Letter Anklet in one metal pairs beautifully with a textured Boho Finger Hand Chain in the other, because they're designed for different purposes and different areas of your body. They're not competing—they're complementing.
Think about the metals you already own and like. If you naturally gravitate toward certain combinations, trust that instinct. You're the expert on what makes you feel good.
Body placement makes mixing easier than you think

When you spread metal mixing across different body zones, it automatically looks intentional. A silver necklace with a gold wrist chain, or a gold shoulder piece with a silver belly chain—these combinations work because they're happening in separate spaces.

The closer two pieces are together, the more they need to match or intentionally contrast. But spread across your body, mixed metals feel curated rather than accidental. A Cross Body Chain in silver can absolutely live alongside a gold anklet or hand chain without any visual clash.
Your jewelry is personal. Wear what makes you feel like yourself, whether that's strict metal matching or a confident mix of both. The confidence matters way more than the rules.

faq.question: Can you wear gold and silver jewelry together?
faq.answer: Yes. The key is balance—let one metal be your dominant choice and use the other as an accent. When you're intentional about the mix, it looks curated instead of random.

faq.answer: Absolutely. Many handmade and designer pieces deliberately combine metals for visual interest. If the piece is designed that way, the metals are meant to work together.

title: How to Measure Yourself for a Plus Size Body Chain
excerpt: Getting the right fit matters. Here's exactly how to measure so your body chain sits perfectly.
content: Body chains are meant to feel good on your skin — not tight, not loose, just right. If you're shopping for a plus size body chain, taking accurate measurements is the difference between a piece you'll actually wear and one that sits in a drawer. We've made hundreds of these by hand, and we've learned what works.

Start with your underbust measurement. Wear an unpadded bra or no bra at all — you want the real you. Wrap a soft measuring tape snugly around your ribcage, just under your bust. Write this number down. This is your baseline. Our Plus Size Body Chain is designed to sit comfortably here, so this measurement matters most.

Next, measure your waist at its narrowest point. For most people, that's slightly above the belly button. Again, keep the tape snug but not tight — imagine the chain sitting there naturally. Body chains should drape, not dig in. If there's a gap between your underbust and waist, note that too. It tells us how your body is shaped, which helps with fit.

Now measure your hip circumference at the fullest part. This matters less for body chains than for anklets or bracelets, but it's helpful to know. Wrap the tape around the widest point of your hips while standing naturally. You're building a complete picture of how the chain will travel down your body.

Here's what most people miss: measure the actual distance from your underbust down to where you want the chain to end. If you like it sitting lower on your hips, measure all the way there. If you prefer a shorter drop, measure less. This is the vertical measurement that determines the overall length you need. Take your time with this one.

Check your measurements twice. Seriously. Do it again tomorrow when you're fresh. Different times of day and different clothing can throw you off by a centimeter or two, and that matters when we're handmaking pieces specifically for you. You're the expert on your own body — trust what you measure.

When you order, you'll choose your size based on these measurements. Our sizing guide matches underbust measurements to our plus size range, and you can always message us directly if you're between sizes or unsure. We're here to help, and we want you to get something that actually fits your life.

title: Keep Your Body Jewelry Looking New: Storage Tips That Work
excerpt: Your favorite chains deserve better than a tangled drawer. Here's how to store them so they stay beautiful.
content: You invested in quality body jewelry for a reason. Whether it's a piece you wear constantly or something special for occasions, proper storage keeps it looking fresh and makes it last. We handmake every single piece here in our Portuguese studio, and we've learned a lot about what keeps jewelry in top condition.

Start with a dry environment. Moisture is the enemy of jewelry longevity, even with high-quality stainless steel that resists tarnish. Keep your pieces in a cool, dry spot away from bathrooms and kitchen sinks. If you live somewhere humid, consider a small dehumidifier or silica gel packets in your storage space. This simple step prevents most damage before it even starts.

Separate your pieces so they don't tangle or scratch each other. A drawer organizer with small compartments works perfectly. If you prefer hanging storage, a jewelry stand or wall hooks keep everything visible and untangled. The Layered Body Chain and delicate pieces especially benefit from being stored separately—they're too beautiful to spend half your morning untangling.

Avoid storing jewelry in plastic bags or boxes without ventilation for long periods. Plastic can trap moisture and potentially react with the metal over time. Use soft cloth pouches or cardboard boxes with tissue paper instead. If a piece came with packaging, that's often ideal for long-term storage.

Keep your jewelry away from direct sunlight and heat sources. Sunlight doesn't damage stainless steel the way it might other metals, but it's still good practice to store in shade. Heat can weaken any adhesive used in charm attachments or gemstone settings, so keep pieces away from radiators, heaters, and warm windowsills.

If you wear your body jewelry daily—which is exactly what high-quality stainless steel is built for—clean it occasionally before storing. A soft cloth is all you need. For pieces like our Pearl Hand Chain or any personalised charm pieces, a gentle wipe removes oils and keeps everything looking pristine. Let it air dry completely before putting it away.

Don't overcrowd your storage space. When jewelry sits too tightly packed, it gets bent, kinked, or damaged. Give each piece room to breathe. This is especially true for delicate chains and layered pieces—they need space to stay in their intended shape. A well-organized drawer might actually hold fewer pieces than you think, but they'll stay perfect.

Check your stored jewelry every few months. A quick look lets you spot any issues early and reminds you of pieces you haven't worn in a while. Rotate what you wear regularly. This spreads the wear across your collection and keeps everything feeling new. Because here's the truth: jewelry made with care deserves to be worn and loved, not locked away forever.

title: How to Layer Necklaces: The Length Rule That Actually Works
excerpt: Layering necklaces doesn't have to look chaotic. Here's the simple principle that makes it work every time.
content: You know the feeling—you want to wear multiple necklaces but end up taking half of them off because they look tangled or messy. The problem isn't that you're doing it wrong. It's just that most people don't know the one rule that makes layering actually work. Once you understand it, you'll be able to combine necklaces with confidence.

The golden rule is simple: vary your lengths. If you're wearing two necklaces, one should sit higher on your neck (shorter) and one lower (longer). This creates visual separation and prevents that awkward clumping effect where everything bunches together in the middle of your chest. Think of it like a staircase—each piece should have its own level.

Start with a choker or short necklace as your base. Something that sits right at the collarbone or just below it works perfectly here. A Pink Cross Choker Necklace or Colorful Crystal Bead Choker gives you that high anchor point. These sit tight enough that they won't slide around when you add more pieces on top.

Next, add a medium-length necklace that falls a few inches lower—somewhere around mid-chest. This is where you have room to play with texture and style. You can mix delicate chains with bolder statement pieces here. The key is that gap between your first and second necklace. That breathing room is what makes the whole look intentional instead of accidental.

For a third layer, go long. Let it fall to your lower chest or even your stomach. This creates maximum visual separation and gives your eye something to follow. A longer chain also feels different from the shorter pieces, so you're not competing with similar lengths. Our Maximalist Layered Necklace Stack is actually three necklaces at different lengths, so you can see this principle in action.

The material matters too, but not in the way you might think. You don't need everything to match or be the same style. In fact, mixing textures—like pairing a delicate chain with a beaded choker or a shell pendant—is what makes layering look personal and intentional. Just make sure your necklaces won't tangle together. high-quality stainless steel chains are perfect because they're lightweight and move independently without getting stuck.

Your neckline affects how this works. High necklines (turtlenecks, crew necks) don't pair well with chokers, so skip the short layer and start with a medium-length piece instead. Lower necklines and off-shoulder tops give you more room to experiment—you can layer three or even four pieces if the lengths are different enough. V-necks are basically the sweet spot for layering. They give you plenty of canvas without fighting your neckline.

Start with just two necklaces if you're new to this. Master the spacing between them first. Once you get comfortable with how different lengths interact, you can add more. title: How to Tell if Your Jewelry is Truly Waterproof
excerpt: Not all jewelry that touches water survives it. Here's what actually makes a piece waterproof—and what doesn't.
content: You've probably bought jewelry labeled 'waterproof' before, only to watch it tarnish or corrode after a few showers. The word gets thrown around so loosely that it's almost meaningless. So let's talk about what waterproof actually means, and how to spot the difference between pieces that'll survive your lifestyle and ones that'll disappoint you.

The material matters more than anything else. Stainless steel—specifically it—is genuinely waterproof because it doesn't rust or tarnish when exposed to water, salt water, or chlorine. That's not a marketing claim; it's chemistry. Most other metals used in jewelry will oxidize or corrode over time. Gold-plating washes away. Silver tarnishes. Even cheaper stainless steel grades contain iron, which rusts. If your jewelry isn't high-quality stainless steel, no amount of coating or sealing will make it truly waterproof.

Coatings and sealants are temporary fixes, not real solutions. You'll see jewelry treated with clear lacquer, resin, or other protective layers marketed as waterproof. The problem? Those coatings wear off. They chip, flake, and fade. Within months or a year, you're back to exposed metal that tarnishes. This is especially true for pieces you wear daily—like body chains or anklets that get constant friction and contact.

Check the clasp and closures too. A waterproof chain means nothing if the clasp corrodes or breaks after a few weeks. Look for solid stainless steel hardware throughout—not just the chain itself. Every connector, jump ring, and fastening point should match the same quality standard. This is where many brands cut corners, and it's where your jewelry fails first.

The Waterproof Belly Chain is waterproof because every single component—chain, hardware, closures—is high-quality stainless steel. No coatings. No gimmicks. It'll survive saltwater swims, daily showers, and years of wear without tarnishing or corroding. That's what true waterproof looks like.

Real talk: if a brand can't tell you the exact material or grade of steel used, walk away. Transparency matters. You should know exactly what you're buying and why it works. Vague descriptions like 'water-resistant' or 'treated for moisture' are red flags. They're admitting the piece isn't actually waterproof—just less likely to fall apart immediately.

Your lifestyle determines what you actually need. If you wear body jewelry daily—to the beach, in the shower, while swimming—you need genuine high-quality stainless steel. Pieces like the Dainty Summer Belly Chain or Zodiac Anklet are built for this because the material itself is waterproof, not treated to be waterproof. If you wear jewelry occasionally and take it off before water activities, you have more flexibility. But why choose less when you can have more?

The best test is time. Buy from brands that back their work and aren't afraid to show you what they're actually using. Every piece we make is high-quality stainless steel because we wear our own jewelry too—and we live in Portugal, where sun, salt air, and water are part of daily life. That's not marketing. That's just knowing what works. Your jewelry should be made to last as long as you want to wear it.

title: Gold Plated vs Gold Tone: What Actually Matters
excerpt: One lasts years. One lasts weeks. Here's how to tell the difference and why it matters for your jewelry.
content: You've probably seen both terms thrown around in jewelry listings. Gold plated. Gold tone. They sound similar enough, right? Wrong. There's actually a massive difference between them, and knowing the distinction will save you money and frustration.

Gold tone is basically paint. It's a thin coating of gold-colored finish applied to base metal — usually brass or stainless steel — through an electroplating process. The coating is so thin (often just a few microns) that it starts wearing off pretty quickly. Rub it the wrong way, sweat on it, shower in it, and you'll see the base metal peeking through within weeks or months.

Gold plating is thicker than gold tone, but not by much. It's still electroplated, but the gold layer is typically 2.5 microns or more — which sounds tiny, but makes a real difference. A properly plated piece will last you 1-3 years with regular wear, depending on how much you're actually wearing it and how you care for it.

Here's the thing: neither gold plating nor gold tone is permanent. They're both designed to wear away eventually. That's just physics. Your body chemistry, your daily habits, even the products you use — they all speed up the process. If you're wearing a gold-plated piece constantly, sweating in it, sleeping in it, showering with it, you're going to see wear faster than someone who takes it off before bed.

So why do brands use these methods at all? Cost and accessibility. Real solid gold jewelry is expensive. Gold plating lets you wear the look you love without breaking the bank. But you need to go in with eyes open about what you're getting and how long it will realistically last.

We chose a different route at Bodystrands. Every piece we make uses high-quality stainless steel — no plating, no coating, no finish that wears away. It's waterproof, it won't tarnish, and you can wear it every single day without worrying about it degrading. Whether you're grabbing our Eyeglasses Chain or the Boho Beach Body Chain, the material stays exactly the same year after year.

If you do choose plated jewelry, here's how to make it last: take it off before you shower, before you sleep, and definitely before you swim or hit the gym. Avoid lotions and perfumes on the areas where the jewelry touches your skin. Store it in a dry place. These habits sound strict, but they genuinely extend the life of the piece.

At the end of the day, it comes down to what you want from your jewelry. If you like switching pieces constantly and don't mind replacing them, plated jewelry is fine. If you want something you can throw on every morning and forget about, reach for durable materials that are built to last. Your wallet and your wrists will thank you.
